h1: Lone Star Tick: Identification, Range Map, Bites, Diseases and Alpha-Gal
dek: How to identify a lone star tick at every life stage with real photos, where CDC records it state by state, the illnesses it can spread, and what a bite means, including the red meat allergy alpha-gal syndrome.
excerpt: How to spot a lone star tick at every life stage, where CDC records it state by state, what its bite can cause, from ehrlichiosis to alpha-gal syndrome, and what to do.

quickAnswer.lead: **A lone star tick is a reddish-brown tick about 1/8 inch long, and the adult female carries one white spot in the middle of her back, the mark [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/lone-star-tick-surveillance.html) uses to tell the species apart.** It bites people aggressively across much of the Northeast, South and Midwest, can spread ehrlichiosis and other illnesses, and is linked to the red meat allergy alpha-gal syndrome, but not to Lyme disease.
bullets: Nymphs are pinhead-sized and larvae, called seed ticks, are about the size of a printed period, according to [University of Illinois Extension](https://hyg.ipm.illinois.edu/article.php?id=465); males have no single spot, only faint white marks around the edge of the back.
CDC's county records through 2025 list the lone star tick as established in 1,139 counties in 33 states and the District of Columbia, from Texas to New Hampshire.
CDC calls it a very aggressive tick that bites humans; nymphs and adult females bite people most often.
It is linked to ehrlichiosis, tularemia, Heartland virus and likely Bourbon virus, and to the STARI rash, while CDC says lone star ticks are not able to transmit Lyme disease bacteria.

In the US, alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to red meat, is primarily associated with lone star tick bites, and reactions usually start 2 to 6 hours after eating red meat or dairy ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/alpha-gal-syndrome/signs-symptoms/index.html)).
Remove an attached tick with fine-tipped tweezers right away, and see a doctor if a rash or fever follows within several weeks ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html)).

body.text: What does a lone star tick look like?

An adult lone star tick is a roundish, reddish-brown tick about 1/8 inch across, and the female carries a single white spot in the middle of her back. [University of Illinois Extension](https://hyg.ipm.illinois.edu/article.php?id=465) gives that size, and the [Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station's Tick Management Handbook](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/publications/bulletins/b1010pdf) measures adults at about 3 to 4 mm and says the species is named for the conspicuous spot at the end of the female's shield.

body.alt: Adult female lone star tick on a green blade of grass, a round reddish-brown body with one white spot near the center of its back and pale-banded legs
body.caption: An adult female lone star tick on a blade of grass, in a CDC photo. The single white spot is the lone star the species is named for.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch; photo: Lauren Bishop (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Up close, [Texas A&M's tick identification guide](https://tickapp.tamu.edu/home/tick-identification/lone-star-tick/) describes the spot as often iridescent and anything from white to cream or gold to bronze, and measures unfed females at 4 to 6 mm, up to about 1/4 inch, a little larger than the Connecticut handbook does. Their long mouthparts are why the bite can hurt, the handbook notes.

Males are marked differently, which trips people up: no single spot, just faint white streaks or spots around the edge of the back, as the Connecticut handbook and the [University of Rhode Island's TickEncounter program](https://web.uri.edu/tickencounter/species/lone-star-tick/) describe. Texas A&M puts males at 2 to 5 mm, under 1/4 inch, fed or not; a male's shield covers almost his whole back, so he barely swells, the handbook explains.

body.alt: Adult male lone star tick seen from above on black, a dark reddish-brown oval with small pale cream marks near the edges of its back and no central white spot
body.caption: An adult male lone star tick, in a CDC photo. Males lack the female's single spot; their pale markings sit around the edge of the back.
body.credit: CDC/ Dr. Amanda Loftis, Dr. William Nicholson, Dr. Will Reeves, Dr. Chris Paddock; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: A fed female looks like a different animal. Texas A&M says she can reach 16 mm, about 5/8 inch, or more; the University of Rhode Island says she needs a week to 10 days or more to fill, and the Connecticut handbook says a female lays 1,000 to 8,000 eggs, about 3,000 on average.

body.alt: Engorged female lone star tick seen from above on black, a swollen gray and cream oval body dotted with tiny pits, with small legs and mouthparts at the front
body.caption: An engorged female lone star tick seen from above, in a CDC photo. CDC notes she was sitting on a clutch of eggs.
body.credit: CDC/ Dr. Amanda Loftis, Dr. William Nicholson, Dr. Will Reeves, Dr. Chris Paddock; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.needed: Unfed adult female and adult male lone star ticks side by side, top view, beside a ruler marked in inches or a US penny, identified by CDC, an extension service or an entomologist; public domain or CC0 so it could also serve as a share image

body.text: What do lone star tick nymphs and larvae look like?

They are much smaller than adults: Illinois Extension calls nymphs pinhead-sized and larvae, the seed ticks, about the size of the period at the end of a sentence. Each of the three active stages, larva, nymph and adult, needs a blood meal, the [University of Kentucky's lone star tick fact sheet](https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef648) says, and Illinois Extension adds that all three feed on people.

body.alt: Four CDC photos in a row labeled adult female, adult male, nymphal and larval lone star tick, shrinking from a large reddish adult to a speck, with the larva also shown enlarged in a circle
body.caption: CDC's lone star tick life stages: adult female, adult male, nymph and larva, with the larva also shown enlarged.
body.credit: CDC, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Count the legs if you can: the Connecticut handbook says larval ticks have six legs, while nymphs and adults have eight. A lone star nymph is round and reddish, more circular than a deer tick nymph, and nymphs are one of the two stages, with adult females, that CDC says bite people most often.

body.alt: Tiny reddish-brown lone star tick nymph crawling near the tip of a person's fingernail, small against the nail
body.caption: A lone star tick nymph crawling on a person's fingernail, in a CDC photo. At this stage the tick is about the size of a pinhead.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Seed ticks often turn up in crowds in late summer. Walking through a patch of newly hatched larvae can leave hundreds on your legs, Illinois Extension says, and the University of Rhode Island notes that lone star larvae latch on by the hundreds. The guide to [seed ticks and how to remove dozens at once](/blog/seed-ticks) covers that situation, including the tape method.

body.alt: Hundreds of tiny reddish-brown seed ticks scattered across white knit fabric, each a speck with legs
body.caption: Hundreds of lone star tick larvae on white knit fabric, from a Virginia observation on iNaturalist that its observer titled a larval tick bomb.
body.credit: (c) Anne Parker, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Lone star tick vs deer tick: how do you tell them apart?

Look at the back. A white spot on a female, or faint white marks around the edge of a male, points to a lone star tick; a plain dark shield with no white points to a blacklegged, or deer, tick. The Connecticut handbook adds that in some places people call the lone star tick a deer tick too, one reason the two get mixed up.

body.text: Two other ticks with pale markings are easy to confuse with it. The American dog tick is bigger, almost 1/4 inch long unfed, with a whitish or silvery-gray pattern on its shield instead of one spot, and short mouthparts, the Connecticut handbook says. The Gulf Coast tick shares the lone star tick's genus and has long, slender mouthparts, but [Ohio State University](https://cfaes-contenthub.org.ohio-state.edu/fact-sheet/gulf-coast-tick-amblyomma-maculatum) describes its shield as decorated with whitish lines. CDC places it mainly in the Southeast and links its adults to *Rickettsia parkeri* rickettsiosis, a form of spotted fever.

To see all three at actual size, the [tick identification chart](/learn/tick-identification-chart) puts the deer tick, dog tick and lone star tick side by side, and [what the common US ticks look like](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like) covers the rest. Still unsure? The [tick species identifier](/tools/tick-identifier) narrows it down from six quick questions.

body.text: Lone star tick map: where in the US does it live?

Across the Northeast, South and Midwest, in [CDC's description of where ticks live](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/about/where-ticks-live.html). CDC's [lone star tick surveillance](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/lone-star-tick-surveillance.html) records, which run through 2025, list the tick as established in 1,139 counties in 33 states and the District of Columbia, and as reported in 635 more. Texas has the most established counties, 118, followed by Kentucky with 86, Arkansas with 73, Virginia with 70 and Oklahoma with 69. In Arkansas it is established in 73 of the state's 75 counties.

Reported means fewer were found. Status is cumulative and depends on sampling, so no record does not mean no ticks. Shares calculated by BuzzSkito.

body.text: Where a state has its own tick page, the map and the list under it link to that state's county map, and [ticks by state](/learn/ticks-by-state) compares every state. At the northern edge, CDC lists the tick as established in Merrimack County, New Hampshire, Dukes County, Massachusetts, and Presque Isle County, Michigan; Maine, Vermont, Minnesota, Colorado, New Mexico and Wyoming have reports but no established county.
Is the lone star tick spreading north?

Its range has moved north since the 1940s, though part of that is a return to old ground. CDC's surveillance page says the tick ranged across the eastern US in the 1750s, receded as forests were cleared and white-tailed deer, a keystone host, declined, and has repopulated its historical range as deer numbers and range grew in the East after the 1940s.

Older descriptions show the change. When the first lone star tick from Delaware was reported in the mid-1940s, Virginia was considered the northern edge of its normal range, a [2021 review in the Delaware Journal of Public Health](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8352541/) recounts; by 2021 it was the tick most often encountered in Delaware. In 2007 the Connecticut handbook put the edge at southern Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Pennsylvania, and at New Jersey and Long Island on the coast. CDC's 2025 records show established counties beyond that line, from upstate New York and New Hampshire to Michigan, Wisconsin and South Dakota.

Two cautions apply. CDC notes that a county often turns established simply because it was sampled for the first time, so a new record does not prove the tick moved, and that ticks reported at the edges may not find conditions stable enough to settle. The Delaware review attributes the expansion to shorter, milder winters and more white-tailed deer, helped by suburbs and forest edges, and cites modeling that predicts further spread north and west.
Where do lone star ticks hide, and how do they find people?

They wait in shady, overgrown places, then come to you. The University of Rhode Island finds them mostly in woodlands with dense undergrowth and around animal resting areas, and the University of Kentucky says numbers run highest along wooded edges, trail margins and overgrown vegetation, where cover protects them from direct sun and hot, dry air.

Unlike ticks that only lie in wait, lone star ticks actively seek hosts, drawn by carbon dioxide and the vibrations of movement, the Delaware review explains, and CDC calls the species a very aggressive tick that bites humans. They crawl fast enough that one may already be waist-high by the time you notice it, the University of Rhode Island says; adults wait on tall grass in shade or the tips of low branches, while nymphs quest lower and latch on between shoe and shin.

body.alt: Small reddish-brown adult female lone star tick crawling on the side of a white leather sneaker near the laces
body.caption: An adult female lone star tick crawling on a white sneaker, in a CDC photo. Check shoes, socks and lower legs after time in tick habitat.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch; photo: Lauren Bishop (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: They are not picky about hosts. The Connecticut handbook says the species feeds on virtually any mammal, and Texas A&M lists deer, cattle, horses, feral swine, sheep, dogs and humans among the hosts of adults. Rodents do not appear to be important hosts for the young ticks, the handbook adds, which matters for yard control further down this page.
When are lone star ticks active?

Mostly from spring through late summer, with each stage peaking at a different time. [CDC's tick bite prevention page](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/prevention/index.html) says ticks in general are most active from April to September, and the University of Kentucky gives March through September for lone star ticks, with nymphs and adults active in spring and larvae abundant in August and September. The season starts earlier in the South and later in the North:

Adults
Nymphs
Larvae (seed ticks)

April to June, then July to August
body.caption: Months vary by year and place. Texas: Texas A&M. Kentucky: University of Kentucky. Delaware: the state survey reported in the Delaware Journal of Public Health, which collected lone star ticks every month from April to November. Connecticut: the CAES handbook.

body.text: The University of Rhode Island gives April to late August for adults. CDC adds that tick exposure can happen year-round, so a tick check after time outdoors is worth doing in any month.
What diseases do lone star ticks carry?

CDC links the lone star tick to ehrlichiosis, tularemia, Heartland virus disease, Bourbon virus disease, a rash illness called STARI and alpha-gal syndrome, a red meat allergy; its guide to where ticks live names two ehrlichiosis bacteria the tick carries, *Ehrlichia chaffeensis* and *Ehrlichia ewingii*. The strength of each link differs, and this table gives it in CDC's terms:

body.text: Ehrlichiosis can be treated: [CDC's ehrlichiosis page](https://www.cdc.gov/ehrlichiosis/about/index.html) says doxycycline is the treatment of choice for adults and children of all ages, so a fever in the weeks after a lone star tick bite is a reason to see a provider.

STARI, short for southern tick-associated rash illness, can look like the Lyme disease rash, sometimes clearing in the middle like a bull's-eye. [CDC's STARI page](https://www.cdc.gov/stari/about/index.html) says it is not caused by the Lyme disease bacterium, its cause is unknown, and it is not known whether antibiotics are necessary or helpful; it occurs most often in the southern US, where Lyme disease is rare.

Both viruses are uncommon: CDC calls Heartland cases rare and reports a limited number of Bourbon cases. [CDC's Heartland virus page](https://www.cdc.gov/heartland-virus/about/index.html) says most cases come from eastern, southeastern and south-central states; [its Bourbon virus page](https://www.cdc.gov/bourbon-virus/about/index.html) says the virus was first identified in Bourbon County, Kansas, in 2014 and has since been reported in the Midwest, on the East Coast and in the South. No medicine treats either virus, and some patients may need hospital care for fluids and symptom relief.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is not on CDC's list for this tick: the Delaware review notes that lone star ticks can transmit its bacterium in the laboratory but that transmission in nature is unconfirmed, though some researchers consider it a strong possibility. For the illnesses other US ticks spread, see the [guide to tick-borne diseases](/learn/tick-borne-diseases).
Do lone star ticks carry Lyme disease?

No. [CDC's page on how Lyme disease spreads](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/causes/index.html) says lone star ticks are not able to transmit Lyme disease bacteria, and neither are American dog ticks, Rocky Mountain wood ticks or brown dog ticks. In the eastern US the blacklegged, or deer, tick spreads it. The Connecticut handbook says the same and ties the lone star tick instead to STARI, the Lyme-like rash described above.

That does not make a lone star bite trivial, since the tick can pass on the other illnesses in the table. If you are unsure which tick bit you, treat a rash or fever as you would after any tick bite, and see [the ticks that carry Lyme disease](/blog/ticks-that-carry-lyme-disease) for photos of the two US species that do.
Can a lone star tick bite cause a red meat allergy?

Yes, in some people. [CDC's alpha-gal syndrome page](https://www.cdc.gov/alpha-gal-syndrome/about/index.html) says that in the US the syndrome is primarily associated with the bite of a lone star tick, and less commonly with blacklegged or western blacklegged ticks, though more research is needed on the role ticks play. People with it react to alpha-gal, a sugar found in most mammals but not in people, apes or Old World monkeys, as the Delaware review explains, so red meat and other mammal products can set off a reaction.

Not everyone who is bitten develops it, and CDC says the reason some people do and others do not is not known. [CDC's symptom page](https://www.cdc.gov/alpha-gal-syndrome/signs-symptoms/index.html) says it can take weeks to months after a bite for symptoms to start, and that reactions usually come 2 to 6 hours after eating red meat or dairy. They range from hives and stomach pain to swelling and trouble breathing.

More than 110,000 suspected cases were identified from 2010 to 2022, CDC says, and as many as 450,000 people may be affected; most reported cases come from southern, eastern and central states, where most lone star ticks are found. A provider diagnoses it from your history, an examination and a test for antibodies to alpha-gal, and CDC says an allergist or other provider should manage it. The [Virginia Department of Health](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/epidemiology/epidemiology-fact-sheets/alpha-gal-syndrome/) says the allergy diminishes over time in some people, particularly without further lone star tick bites. The [guide to alpha-gal syndrome](/blog/alpha-gal-syndrome) covers the foods involved and living with it.

body.title: Severe reaction after a meal
body.text: CDC says to seek immediate emergency care for a severe allergic reaction or anaphylaxis; its symptom list includes difficulty breathing, swelling of the lips, throat, tongue or eyelids, and dizziness or faintness. If you think you may have alpha-gal syndrome, talk to your health care provider.
What does a lone star tick bite look like?

It can leave a red, itchy spot that may last two weeks or longer, the University of Kentucky says, because substances in the tick's saliva cause a reaction. CDC notes the same irritation and says redness and discomfort at the bite do not necessarily mean an infection. The Connecticut handbook adds that the bite can be painful because of the long mouthparts.

A red patch that keeps spreading is different. A rash that appears around the bite, usually within 7 days, and expands to 3 to 12 inches across fits CDC's description of STARI, and CDC advises seeing a doctor for any rash or fever in the weeks after a tick bite. For photos of ordinary bites day by day, see [what a tick bite looks like](/blog/what-does-a-tick-bite-look-like).

body.needed: The STARI rash: a red, expanding rash around a confirmed lone star tick bite, from CDC or a university medical source, public domain or CC0, with its size and the days since the bite on record; placed low on the page

body.text: Check the places they favor. In tick-testing records from Delaware, the most common attachment sites on people were the upper leg and groin, about 19% each, then the lower leg and back, about 12% each, and the armpit, about 6%, the Delaware review reports.
What should you do after a lone star tick bite?

Remove the tick as soon as you find it, then watch your health for several weeks. [CDC's steps for removing a tick](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html) are the same for every species:

items: Grasp the tick with clean, fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin as you can, without squeezing its body.
Pull the tick away from the skin with steady, even pressure; twisting or jerking can leave the mouthparts in the skin.
If the mouthparts break off, remove them with tweezers only if that is easy; otherwise leave them and let the skin heal.
Clean the bite and your hands with soap and water, rubbing alcohol or hand sanitizer, and check your body for other ticks.
Get rid of a live tick by sealing it in a bag or container, wrapping it tightly in tape, flushing it or putting it in alcohol; never crush it with your fingers.

body.alt: Fine-tipped tweezer points gripping a small reddish lone star tick at the skin in the crook of a person's elbow
body.caption: Fine-tipped tweezers removing an adult female lone star tick from a person's elbow, in a CDC photo. Grip close to the skin and pull away with steady, even pressure.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch; photo: Lauren Bishop (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Skip the folk remedies: CDC advises against petroleum jelly, nail polish, heat or similar tricks to make a tick detach. It also generally advises against having the tick tested, because results can be unreliable and a negative result can falsely reassure. If mouthparts stay in the skin, see [what to do about a tick head stuck in skin](/blog/tick-head-stuck-in-skin), and the [step-by-step tick removal guide](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-safely) goes through removal in more detail.

Then watch your health. CDC says to see a doctor if a rash or fever develops within several weeks of removing a tick, and to tell the doctor about the bite, when it happened and where you most likely picked up the tick. After a lone star bite, also notice any allergic reaction a few hours after eating red meat in the weeks or months that follow. [What to do after a tick bite](/blog/tick-bite-what-to-do) covers the same steps for any tick.

body.title: When to see a health care provider
body.text: See a provider if a rash or fever appears within several weeks of a tick bite, and say that a tick bit you. Seek emergency care for a severe allergic reaction. This page summarizes CDC guidance and is not a diagnosis.
How do you prevent lone star tick bites?
Treat clothing, use repellent and check yourself after time outdoors. CDC's general prevention advice applies to lone star ticks too:

items: **Treat clothing and gear with 0.5% permethrin**, or buy pretreated items, following the label.

**Use an EPA-registered repellent** containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD) or 2-undecanone, as the label directs, and do not use OLE or PMD on children under 3.
**Stay in the center of trails** and out of the grassy, brushy and wooded areas where ticks wait.
**Check clothing, gear and pets** when you come in, and put dry clothes in the dryer on high heat for 10 minutes to kill ticks on them.

**Shower within two hours** of coming indoors and check your whole body, including under the arms, in and around the ears and hair, inside the belly button, the backs of the knees, between the legs and around the waist.

body.text: There is lone-star-specific support for the first two: the Delaware review cites field studies in which permethrin-treated clothing and DEET sprays protected people against lone star ticks.

In the yard, CDC suggests removing leaf litter, clearing tall grass and brush, mowing often and laying a 3-foot strip of wood chips or gravel between lawns and woods. If you also spray, [the best tick sprays for a yard](/blog/best-tick-spray-for-yard) lists the EPA-registered options and where to apply them. Clearing leaf litter where people and pets spend time may also cut lone star tick survival over winter, since the ticks rely on humid spots, the Delaware review notes; it adds that tick tubes and rodent bait boxes, developed with blacklegged ticks in mind, suit lone star ticks poorly because they do not feed mainly on rodents. [What kills ticks in the yard and on clothes](/blog/what-kills-ticks) compares the options.
Pets need checking too: lone star ticks bite dogs, and [how to check a dog for ticks](/blog/ticks-on-dogs) shows where they hide in a coat. Ask a veterinarian which tick preventive suits your pet.

body.title: Save the tick, or a photo of it
body.text: Before you get rid of a tick, photograph it from above on a white surface beside a ruler marked in inches, and note the date and place. The University of Rhode Island's free [TickSpotters](https://web.uri.edu/tickencounter/tickspotters/) program identifies ticks from a photo, usually by email within 24 hours, and your state's cooperative extension office may also help. If you get sick, tell your doctor about the bite.

faqs.question: What happens if you get bitten by a lone star tick?
faqs.answer: At the bite you may get a red, itchy spot: CDC says lone star tick saliva can be irritating, so redness does not necessarily mean infection, and the University of Kentucky says the itch can last two weeks or longer. Less often the bite passes on an illness such as ehrlichiosis, which starts with fever and chills 1 to 2 weeks later, or is followed by STARI, an expanding rash. Some people later develop alpha-gal syndrome. Remove the tick promptly and see a doctor if a rash or fever appears within several weeks.

faqs.question: Do all lone star ticks cause meat allergy?
faqs.answer: No. CDC says not every person bitten by a lone star tick develops alpha-gal syndrome, and that the reason some people do and others do not is not known. In the United States the syndrome is primarily associated with lone star tick bites, and less commonly with blacklegged or western blacklegged ticks. Symptoms can take weeks to months to appear after a bite, and reactions usually start 2 to 6 hours after eating red meat or dairy. If that pattern sounds familiar, talk to a health care provider.

faqs.question: Does every lone star tick carry Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: No lone star tick spreads Lyme disease. CDC says lone star ticks are not able to transmit the bacteria that cause it; in the eastern United States the blacklegged, or deer, tick does. A lone star tick can carry other germs, including those behind ehrlichiosis, tularemia and Heartland virus disease, and its bite is associated with STARI, a rash that can look like the Lyme disease rash but has a different, unknown cause. A rash or fever after any tick bite is still a reason to see a provider.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get sick from a lone star tick bite?
faqs.answer: It depends on the illness. CDC says ehrlichiosis symptoms begin 1 to 2 weeks after the bite, the STARI rash usually appears within 7 days, and Heartland virus disease can start anywhere from a few days to several weeks later. Alpha-gal syndrome works differently: it can take weeks to months after a bite for symptoms to start, and the allergic reactions then come 2 to 6 hours after eating red meat or dairy. CDC advises seeing a doctor for a rash or fever within several weeks of a tick bite.

faqs.question: What are the odds of getting a disease from a lone star tick?
faqs.answer: No national figure exists in the sources used here, and the odds vary by place and germ. In Delaware, a 2021 review reported that about 1.5% of the lone star ticks people submitted to an Army laboratory between 1998 and 2019 tested positive for a germ, and about 2% of those sent to a university lab from 2008 to 2020. CDC also notes that not everyone bitten develops alpha-gal syndrome. Low odds are not zero, so watch for a rash or fever for several weeks after a bite.

faqs.question: Does the meat allergy from a lone star tick bite ever go away?
faqs.answer: It can fade for some people. The Virginia Department of Health says that in some people the allergy will diminish over time, particularly if there are no further lone star tick bites, which is one more reason to avoid them. CDC says alpha-gal syndrome should be managed under the care of an allergist or other health care provider, so talk with that provider before trying red meat or dairy again rather than testing it on your own.

faqs.question: How can I tell the difference between a lone star tick and a regular tick?
faqs.answer: Look at the back. An adult female lone star tick has one white spot in the middle of her back, and a male has faint white marks around the edge. The blacklegged, or deer, tick has a plain dark shield with no white, and the American dog tick is larger, almost 1/4 inch unfed, with a whitish or silvery-gray pattern across the shield. Lone star adults are reddish brown and about 1/8 inch long, with long mouthparts. Nymphs are pinhead-sized and harder to sort, so a clear photo helps.

faqs.question: How big is a lone star tick?
faqs.answer: An unfed adult is about 1/8 inch long, according to University of Illinois Extension and the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, which measures adults at 3 to 4 mm. Texas A&M measures unfed females at 4 to 6 mm and males at 2 to 5 mm, and says a fully fed female can reach 16 mm, about 5/8 inch, or more. Nymphs are about the size of a pinhead, and larvae, the seed ticks, are about the size of a printed period.

faqs.question: Where are lone star ticks found in the United States?
faqs.answer: Mostly in the Northeast, South and Midwest, in CDC's description. CDC's county records through 2025 list the tick as established in 1,139 counties in 33 states and the District of Columbia, led by Texas, Kentucky, Arkansas, Virginia and Oklahoma, and as reported but not established in Maine, Vermont, Minnesota, Colorado, New Mexico and Wyoming. It favors woodlands with dense undergrowth, wooded edges and overgrown areas, and CDC cautions that a county with no record may simply not have been sampled.

faqs.question: Do lone star ticks bite dogs and cats?
faqs.answer: Yes. Texas A&M lists dogs among the hosts of adult lone star ticks, and a 2021 review in the Delaware Journal of Public Health says they usually attach to a dog's belly, armpits or groin and to a cat's tail and rear end. The same review says lone star ticks can carry bacteria that cause ehrlichiosis in dogs and a parasite, Cytauxzoon felis, that causes a serious illness in cats. Check pets after time outdoors and ask a veterinarian about tick prevention.
